To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the suppressive activity of CD4(+) regulatory T (Treg) cells is transferred to conventional CD4+ T helper (Th)-cells via cell-cell contact.

human CD25( + ) regulatory T cells convey suppression of conventional CD25( - ) T cells via cell-cell contact and soluble transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta) and that the suppressive properties of CD25( -) T cells can be induced by CD25( +) Treg cells via a mechanism that is termed 'infectious tolerance'.
CD25(+) human regulatory T cells suppress the activation of CD4+ T cells in a cell contact-dependent manner.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of regulatory T cells in autoimmune disease and cancer.
the molecular and cellular basis of the phenomenon of infectious suppressive activity.
the mechanisms underlying the induction of suppressive activity in conventional T helper cells by human CD4(+) regulatory T (Treg) cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

CD25(+) human Treg cells can suppress the proliferation of conventional CD4(+)-T cells by two different mechanisms, namely, a contact-dependent and a contact-independent mechanism, which are both TGF-beta dependent.

CD25(+)CD4(+) Treg-mediated suppressive activity is a complex, multi-component process, which involves cell contact, cell-cell contact-independent soluble factors, such as TGF-beta and IL-10, and the activation status of the Treg cells.
the suppression of CD25( + ) Treg cells is mediated by cell contact, whereas the transfer of suppression to other cells requires TGF-beta.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CD25(+)Treg cell-mediated suppression is not mediated by membrane-bound TGF-b, but that it is partially mediated by soluble TGF-b.
Treg cells can transfer their suppressive activity to conventional CD25(-) T cells via cell contact and that these cells are anergic and secrete soluble TGF-beta.

Treg cells suppress CD4+ T helper cells in an antigen-nonspecific manner by a mechanism that involves cell contact, cell-cell contact-dependent induction of anergy in conventional CD4+ T cells, and cell-contact-independent transfer of suppressor activity from anergic to freshly isolated CD4+ T cell.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Treg cells can suppress conventional T cells by transferring suppressive properties to these conventional T cells.
the suppressive properties of CD25(?) Tregs are transferred to CD25(+) Th cells.
the suppressive function of CD4(+) CD25(+) cells is not only cell contact-dependent but also cell contact-independent, and that the cell contact-independent suppression requires TGF-beta.
